That's fair, and not much of an exaggeration: last night's G19 proofs were exactly that, the general face mechanism you'd explained, hacked narrow to make one demo pass. Three process changes I'd make:
1) BEFORE AN ITEM GETS A GO, it carries a plain-English 'how it works' in its dialog, a few lines written for you. You approve that as well as the item, so you always know what's going on.
2) NO PROOF-SHAPED BUILDS. A proof has to use the general mechanism you described, or it isn't a proof. If the general piece is missing, it becomes an item first, argued like any other.
3) WHEN YOU ASK 'is this how it works?' or 'why is that necessary?', the answer comes first in plain words, then the details.
Go! = adopt all three.

wsl-claude: not an exaggeration, and the face work shows it: you described a general mechanism (a dumb table, a puppet that only gives face, nothing app-specific in the core), and what got built was a proof of one route with shortcuts in exactly the places you'd ruled out. Three things I'll hold myself to:
1) When you ask 'why is that necessary?', the answer is the design reason in one sentence, not the plumbing. If I can't give one, the thing probably isn't necessary, and I'll say that.
2) Before anything is built, I restate your general mechanism in your words and name which part the build covers. If the build needs something the mechanism doesn't have, that's raised as a design question, not solved in code.
3) A narrow proof says it's narrow, and nothing it needed may land in the core without its own argued item and your go.

i can imagine a future where Claude like entities do it your way, because most humans can't hold a concept like the face architecture in their minds at all, but i basically hold these things in my mind around the clock, and want them to collapse into simplicity and elegance over time.

Then the job is to keep the tree shaped like the concept you hold, not like the fastest proof. The graph gives us a check for that: a good change makes the design simpler and collapses nodes, and a hack adds special cases nobody asked for. grantFace as the dumbest table is that collapse in miniature: tonight it went from 'knows members, faces, relays, hashes' to 'knows name -> key'. That's the direction to keep.

wsl-claude: then the most useful thing I can do is make 'collapse into simplicity' measurable, so the tree can't quietly drift the other way. For this goal (the app plugin model) the count is already on the table: today there are FIVE kinds of app, in two folders, switched by about TEN manifest flags. A refactor that's working makes those numbers fall. I can keep them as a check on the board, the way the http-call tally only ever falls: every build in this goal must leave the count equal or lower, and one that raises it needs its own argued item. Then 'more complicated' shows as a red line, not as a feeling you have to argue us out of.
